title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 6.4.1 Writing: Creative Writing (Pictorial Compositions)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A pictorial composition is a short story written from pictures. In this sub-strand you will put pictures about email and the internet into a sensible order, write about 60 to 80 words from them, and choose other pictures safely when you want a new topic.

## Strand 6.0: Internet - Email
Sub-strand 6.4.1: Writing: Creative Writing (Pictorial Compositions)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) organise pictures in a logical sequence to write pictorial compositions of about 60-80 words on the theme
b) write a pictorial composition of about 60 - 80 words on the theme for effective communication
c) adopt the use of a wide range of pictures to write pictorial compositions on different topics for communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Pictorial Compositions

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do pictures make you feel?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is developed as the learner collaboratively discusses and uses pictures to write composition.
• Digital Literacy: This is enhanced as the learner uses digital devices to view pictures online and write compositions.

## Values
• Unity: This is promoted as the learner collaborates harmoniously with peers in groups to discuss pictures and watch videos related to the theme.
• Respect: This is cultivated as the learner engages with peers mutually and accommodates others opinion on varied issues.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Cyber Safety: It is promoted as the learners use internet responsibly to access pictures and visuals for composition writing.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of pictorial compositions to their learning in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 6.0 Internet-Email, Sub-strand 6.4.1 Creative Writing: Pictorial Compositions

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Putting pictures in order

LESSON 1: PUTTING PICTURES IN ORDER
===================================

## What you will learn
• Say what is happening in each picture before you write.
• Arrange pictures so the story moves from start to finish.
• Explain why one order is more logical than another.

Curriculum outcomes: a) organise pictures in a logical sequence to write pictorial compositions of about 60-80 words on the theme

## Introduction
Four pictures can tell a story only if they stand in the right queue. If the reply arrives before the email is written, the reader cannot trust the writer.

## Notes
### Look before you order
A pictorial composition begins with looking, not with writing. For each picture, say:

- Who is in it?
- Where are they?
- What are they doing?
- What might have happened just before, and what might happen next?

Use only what you can see, plus a sensible link between pictures. Do not invent a crash, a prize or a private address that no picture shows.

### Four pictures about an email
Picture A. A girl and her aunt sit at a computer. The girl points at a button labelled Compose.
Picture B. The girl types. The aunt points at an email address on a slip of paper.
Picture C. The girl's finger is near Send. Both of them are looking at the address on the screen.
Picture D. The girl smiles. A new line in the inbox shows that a reply has arrived. The aunt nods.

The logical order is A, B, C, D. She prepares to write, she types and checks the address, she sends, and then a reply comes. Order D, A, C, B would make the reply appear before the typing, which does not make sense.

### Clues that lock the order
Compose comes before a finished message. Checking the address comes before Send. A reply cannot arrive before something was sent, unless the picture is clearly about an older message. In this set, the smile and the inbox belong at the end.

If two orders seem possible, choose the one you can tell in words without adding 'suddenly everything went backwards'. Logical order is the order a careful person would live through.

### From order to notes
Write one short note under each picture, not a full story yet.

A. Open Compose with an adult.
B. Type the message and the address.
C. Check, then send.
D. A reply arrives.

Those notes are the bones of a 60 to 80 word composition. The next lesson puts sentences on them.

## Key words
• pictorial composition — a piece of writing that tells a story based on a series of pictures
• logical order — an order in which each step follows sensibly from the one before
• compose — to start writing a new email

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why can Picture D not come first?

Working:
1. Picture D shows a reply in the inbox.
2. A reply comes after a message has been sent.

Answer: The reply has to follow the sending, so D belongs at the end.

### Example 2
Which picture shows the safety check?

Working:
1. Look for the moment when they study the address before sending.
2. That is Picture C.

Answer: Picture C

## Activity: Order the four pictures
You will need: Four picture cards of the email story, labelled on the back only, Paper for notes
1. In a group, lay the pictures out in the order you first think is right.
2. Each learner describes one picture in a single sentence.
3. Agree on a final order and write a four-line note plan.
4. Explain to another group why Compose cannot follow the reply.

## Practice
1. What four questions help you read one picture?
2. Write the correct order of Pictures A, B, C and D.
3. Why is checking the address before Send a logical step?

## Summary
• Describe each picture before you decide the order.
• Compose, type, check, send, then reply is a logical email story.
• Notes under the pictures become the plan for the composition.

### Answers to practice
1. Who is in it? Where are they? What are they doing? What might come before and after?
2. A, B, C, D
3. It stops the message from going to the wrong person. The picture of Send comes after the typing and before the reply.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Writing 60 to 80 words from pictures

LESSON 2: WRITING 60 TO 80 WORDS FROM PICTURES
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Turn a four-picture plan into a short composition.
• Keep the writing between about 60 and 80 words.
• Use linking words so the pictures feel like one story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) organise pictures in a logical sequence to write pictorial compositions of about 60-80 words on the theme; b) write a pictorial composition of about 60 - 80 words on the theme for effective communication

## Introduction
A picture will not write the sentences for you. It gives you the events. You still choose the words, the order and the length.

## Notes
### From notes to a story
Take the four notes from the email pictures and join them with linking words: one afternoon, first, then, after that, soon.

Name the people once, then use she or they. Stay in the past tense if the pictures show a finished afternoon. Mention the adult, because the pictures include the aunt. Do not add a password, a home address or a strange link. The pictures do not show those things, and they are not safe extras.

### A model
The model below is the length you are aiming for. Count the story, not the title.

A Reply in the Inbox

One afternoon Awuor sat with her aunt at the computer. She wanted to email her cousin. First she clicked Compose and typed the address carefully. Then she wrote a short, polite note about the music festival. Her aunt checked the address with her. After that, Awuor clicked Send. Soon a reply arrived in the inbox. Awuor was glad she had asked an adult before she used the internet.

Read it against the pictures. Compose is there. Typing is there. The check and Send are there. The reply is there. Nothing important has been skipped, and nothing unsafe has been added.

### Hitting the word count
Write your own version about the same pictures or about a similar set your teacher shows you. Change the name, the reason for the email, or the simile-free detail so the piece is yours. You do not have to copy the model.

Count every word in the story. If you are under 60, add one sentence you can actually see, such as the smile or the nod. If you are over 80, remove a repeated idea. Keep a beginning, a middle and an ending.

### A last read
Ask: would a reader who never saw the pictures still understand what happened? If yes, the composition works. If the reader would not know why an adult is there, put the adult back in.

## Key words
• linking word — a word such as first, then or soon that joins events
• word count — the number of words in the story, not counting the title
• model — an example you can learn from without copying it word for word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The draft never mentions Send, but Picture C shows it. What should the writer do?

Working:
1. Every important picture needs a place in the story.
2. Add a short sentence about checking the address and clicking Send.

Answer: Add a sentence for Picture C so the reply has a reason to arrive.

### Example 2
The draft is 95 words because it explains how to build a computer. What should go?

Working:
1. The pictures are about sending an email, not about building a machine.
2. Cut the extra explanation.

Answer: Cut the building explanation and keep the email story near 60 to 80 words.

## Activity: Write from the picture plan
You will need: The ordered pictures or the diagram, Exercise books
1. Discuss the pictures once more and agree the order.
2. Each learner writes a composition of about 60 to 80 words. Include the adult and the four steps.
3. Count the words. Adjust the draft.
4. Read two compositions aloud. The class says which picture each sentence matches.

## Practice
1. Does the title count in the 60 to 80 words?
2. Name the four actions the email pictures should lead you to mention.
3. Why should you not add a password to this story?
4. What can you add if the story is only 45 words long?

## Summary
• Join the pictures with linking words and the past tense.
• Aim for about 60 to 80 words, not counting the title.
• Include what the pictures show, including the adult and the safety check.

### Answers to practice
1. No. Count the words of the story only.
2. Opening Compose, typing the address and message, checking and sending, and receiving a reply.
3. The pictures do not show one, and a password should not be written in a message or shared in a story as if that were safe.
4. One true detail from the pictures, such as the aunt checking the address or the smile when the reply arrives.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Using many kinds of pictures safely

LESSON 3: USING MANY KINDS OF PICTURES SAFELY
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Choose drawings, photographs or video scenes as starting points for writing.
• Write a short pictorial composition on a new but familiar topic.
• Follow cyber-safety rules when pictures come from the internet.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write a pictorial composition of about 60 - 80 words on the theme for effective communication; c) adopt the use of a wide range of pictures to write pictorial compositions on different topics for communication

## Introduction
Once you can write from four email pictures, you can write from a market photograph, a road-safety poster or a short video. The skill stays the same. The safety rules change only when the picture comes from a screen.

## Notes
### Pictures you can use
A wide range means more than one kind.

- A drawing or comic your teacher gives you
- A photograph in a textbook or newspaper
- A poster about road safety or a balanced meal
- A paused moment from a video the class watches together
- A picture you took of your own schoolwork, with permission

For any set, order the moments, name what you see, and write about 60 to 80 words. A poster with one picture can still give a composition if you describe the scene, the choice a person makes, and the result.

### A second topic, still in order
Imagine three pictures of a different afternoon.

1. Learners watch a short video of a footbridge with their teacher.
2. They draw the bridge and a railway crossing in their books.
3. They pin the drawings on the wall and explain them.

A composition from those pictures might say: Our teacher played a short video of a footbridge. First we watched quietly. Then we drew the bridge and a railway crossing. After that we pinned the drawings on the wall and told the class why we should cross only when the way is safe. The pictures helped us remember the lesson.

Count a draft like that and stretch or trim it into the 60 to 80 word range if your teacher asks for that length.

### Cyber safety
If you look for pictures on the internet, do it with a teacher or parent. Use a site they have opened. Do not download files from a stranger. Do not click a picture that leads to a prize or a request for your address. Do not copy a classmate's face into your story online without asking. School writing can use drawings and printed pictures when no device is free.

Give a simple credit when you know the source: 'Photograph from our class textbook' or 'Drawing by our group'. You do not need a long bibliography. You do need honesty about what you saw.

Feelings belong in the writing too. A picture of a reply arriving may make you write that Awuor was glad. A picture of a busy road may make you write that the children were careful. Name the feeling you can defend from the picture, and respect a partner who reads the same picture a little differently.

## Key words
• photograph — a picture taken with a camera
• source — the place a picture or fact came from
• cyber safety — habits that keep you safer when you use the internet
• credit — a short note that says where a picture came from

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A search result shows a bright 'You have won' picture and asks you to click. Should you use it for a composition?

Working:
1. It is an unknown prize lure, not a class picture.
2. Tell an adult and choose a picture the teacher has approved.

Answer: No. Do not click it. Use an approved drawing, textbook photo or class video still.

### Example 2
How is a video still like a picture in a composition?

Working:
1. A paused video gives one moment you can describe.
2. Several pauses can be ordered like several pictures.

Answer: You describe what you see in that moment, and you can order several moments into a story.

## Activity: A new set of pictures
You will need: Textbook pictures, drawings, or a short video the teacher plays, Paper
1. As a group, choose three or four pictures from class materials, or watch a short approved video and sketch three moments.
2. Order them and discuss what feeling each one suggests.
3. Each learner writes about 60 to 80 words. Add a one-line credit for the source.
4. If anyone found a picture online, they explain who opened the site and why they did not click unknown links.

## Practice
1. Name two kinds of pictures you can write from besides a computer drawing.
2. What should you do before you search for pictures on the internet?
3. What is a simple credit?
4. Why can two learners describe the same picture with slightly different feelings?

## Summary
• Drawings, photographs, posters and video stills can all start a composition.
• Keep the story about 60 to 80 words and in logical order.
• Use the internet for pictures only with an adult, and say where the picture came from.

### Answers to practice
1. A textbook photograph, a poster, a newspaper picture, a comic, or a paused video. Any two are acceptable.
2. Ask a teacher or parent and use a site they have opened. Do not download from strangers or click prize links.
3. A short note such as 'Drawing by our group' or 'Photograph from our class textbook'.
4. A picture can suggest more than one careful reading. They should still stick to what the picture shows and listen to each other.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 6.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (PICTORIAL COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Before writing a pictorial composition you should
   A. hide the pictures
   B. say what each picture shows and put them in order
   C. click every link on the page
   D. write the ending first and ignore the drawings

2. In the email pictures, which order is logical?
   A. Reply, send, compose, type
   B. Compose, type, check and send, reply
   C. Send, then compose, then delete the adult
   D. Inbox first, with no message written

3. Picture C, with a finger near Send, belongs
   A. before anyone opens Compose
   B. after typing and before the reply
   C. after the story has ended
   D. in a different subject

4. The story part of the composition should be about
   A. 60 to 80 words
   B. 6 words
   C. 600 words
   D. a password and a home address

5. Which sentence best links two pictures?
   A. First she clicked Compose. Then she typed the address.
   B. Computer computer computer.
   C. Password is 1234 and my home is here.
   D. Suddenly the reply arrived before she wrote.

6. If a draft is far too long, the writer should
   A. add another unrelated story
   B. cut repeated ideas and stay with the pictures
   C. include a stranger's phone number
   D. remove all the verbs

7. A video the class watches can help you write because
   A. you can order moments you saw
   B. you should copy any link in the corner
   C. videos replace all sentences
   D. you must download unknown files

8. Looking online for pictures is safer when
   A. you click every prize you see
   B. a teacher or parent opens an approved site and stays with you
   C. you send your address to get a download
   D. you use a stranger's password

9. A credit in this lesson is
   A. a loan of money
   B. a short note saying where the picture came from
   C. a password
   D. the inbox

10. Write one sentence that could match a picture of an adult and a child checking an email address.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 6.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (PICTORIAL COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

1. B. say what each picture shows and put them in order
   Looking and ordering come before the sentences.

2. B. Compose, type, check and send, reply
   A reply arrives only after a message has been composed and sent.

3. B. after typing and before the reply
   Checking and sending sit between the typing and the reply.

4. A. 60 to 80 words
   That is the length for this sub-strand. The title is extra.

5. A. First she clicked Compose. Then she typed the address.
   First and Then keep the pictures in a possible order without sharing private information.

6. B. cut repeated ideas and stay with the pictures
   The composition should stay near 60 to 80 words and follow the pictures.

7. A. you can order moments you saw
   Paused moments work like pictures in a sequence.

8. B. a teacher or parent opens an approved site and stays with you
   Cyber safety means an adult chooses the site and you avoid unknown links.

9. B. a short note saying where the picture came from
   Honesty about the source is enough at this level.

10. Awuor and her aunt checked the address before she clicked Send.
   The sentence names the people and the safety check the picture shows.

A Reply in the Inbox

One afternoon Awuor sat with her aunt at the computer. She wanted to email her cousin. First she clicked Compose and typed the address carefully. Then she wrote a short, polite note about the music festival. Her aunt checked the address with her. After that, Awuor clicked Send. Soon a reply arrived in the inbox. Awuor was glad she had asked an adult before she used the internet.

Read it against the pictures. Compose is there. Typing is there. The check and Send are there. The reply is there. Nothing important has been skipped, and nothing unsafe has been added.

### Hitting the word count
Write your own version about the same pictures or about a similar set your teacher shows you. Change the name, the reason for the email, or the simile-free detail so the piece is yours. You do not have to copy the model.

Count every word in the story. If you are under 60, add one sentence you can actually see, such as the smile or the nod. If you are over 80, remove a repeated idea. Keep a beginning, a middle and an ending.

### A last read
Ask: would a reader who never saw the pictures still understand what happened? If yes, the composition works. If the reader would not know why an adult is there, put the adult back in.

## Key words
• linking word — a word such as first, then or soon that joins events
• word count — the number of words in the story, not counting the title
• model — an example you can learn from without copying it word for word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The draft never mentions Send, but Picture C shows it. What should the writer do?

Working:
1. Every important picture needs a place in the story.
2. Add a short sentence about checking the address and clicking Send.

Answer: Add a sentence for Picture C so the reply has a reason to arrive.

### Example 2
The draft is 95 words because it explains how to build a computer. What should go?

Working:
1. The pictures are about sending an email, not about building a machine.
2. Cut the extra explanation.

Answer: Cut the building explanation and keep the email story near 60 to 80 words.

## Activity: Write from the picture plan
You will need: The ordered pictures or the diagram, Exercise books
1. Discuss the pictures once more and agree the order.
2. Each learner writes a composition of about 60 to 80 words. Include the adult and the four steps.
3. Count the words. Adjust the draft.
4. Read two compositions aloud. The class says which picture each sentence matches.

## Practice
1. Does the title count in the 60 to 80 words?
2. Name the four actions the email pictures should lead you to mention.
3. Why should you not add a password to this story?
4. What can you add if the story is only 45 words long?

## Summary
• Join the pictures with linking words and the past tense.
• Aim for about 60 to 80 words, not counting the title.
• Include what the pictures show, including the adult and the safety check.

### Answers to practice
1. No. Count the words of the story only.
2. Opening Compose, typing the address and message, checking and sending, and receiving a reply.
3. The pictures do not show one, and a password should not be written in a message or shared in a story as if that were safe.
4. One true detail from the pictures, such as the aunt checking the address or the smile when the reply arrives.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Using many kinds of pictures safely
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: USING MANY KINDS OF PICTURES SAFELY
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Choose drawings, photographs or video scenes as starting points for writing.
• Write a short pictorial composition on a new but familiar topic.
• Follow cyber-safety rules when pictures come from the internet.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write a pictorial composition of about 60 - 80 words on the theme for effective communication; c) adopt the use of a wide range of pictures to write pictorial compositions on different topics for communication

## Introduction
Once you can write from four email pictures, you can write from a market photograph, a road-safety poster or a short video. The skill stays the same. The safety rules change only when the picture comes from a screen.

## Notes
### Pictures you can use
A wide range means more than one kind.

- A drawing or comic your teacher gives you
- A photograph in a textbook or newspaper
- A poster about road safety or a balanced meal
- A paused moment from a video the class watches together
- A picture you took of your own schoolwork, with permission

For any set, order the moments, name what you see, and write about 60 to 80 words. A poster with one picture can still give a composition if you describe the scene, the choice a person makes, and the result.

### A second topic, still in order
Imagine three pictures of a different afternoon.

1. Learners watch a short video of a footbridge with their teacher.
2. They draw the bridge and a railway crossing in their books.
3. They pin the drawings on the wall and explain them.

A composition from those pictures might say: Our teacher played a short video of a footbridge. First we watched quietly. Then we drew the bridge and a railway crossing. After that we pinned the drawings on the wall and told the class why we should cross only when the way is safe. The pictures helped us remember the lesson.

Count a draft like that and stretch or trim it into the 60 to 80 word range if your teacher asks for that length.

### Cyber safety
If you look for pictures on the internet, do it with a teacher or parent. Use a site they have opened. Do not download files from a stranger. Do not click a picture that leads to a prize or a request for your address. Do not copy a classmate's face into your story online without asking. School writing can use drawings and printed pictures when no device is free.

Give a simple credit when you know the source: 'Photograph from our class textbook' or 'Drawing by our group'. You do not need a long bibliography. You do need honesty about what you saw.

Feelings belong in the writing too. A picture of a reply arriving may make you write that Awuor was glad. A picture of a busy road may make you write that the children were careful. Name the feeling you can defend from the picture, and respect a partner who reads the same picture a little differently.

## Key words
• photograph — a picture taken with a camera
• source — the place a picture or fact came from
• cyber safety — habits that keep you safer when you use the internet
• credit — a short note that says where a picture came from

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A search result shows a bright 'You have won' picture and asks you to click. Should you use it for a composition?

Working:
1. It is an unknown prize lure, not a class picture.
2. Tell an adult and choose a picture the teacher has approved.

Answer: No. Do not click it. Use an approved drawing, textbook photo or class video still.

### Example 2
How is a video still like a picture in a composition?

Working:
1. A paused video gives one moment you can describe.
2. Several pauses can be ordered like several pictures.

Answer: You describe what you see in that moment, and you can order several moments into a story.

## Activity: A new set of pictures
You will need: Textbook pictures, drawings, or a short video the teacher plays, Paper
1. As a group, choose three or four pictures from class materials, or watch a short approved video and sketch three moments.
2. Order them and discuss what feeling each one suggests.
3. Each learner writes about 60 to 80 words. Add a one-line credit for the source.
4. If anyone found a picture online, they explain who opened the site and why they did not click unknown links.

## Practice
1. Name two kinds of pictures you can write from besides a computer drawing.
2. What should you do before you search for pictures on the internet?
3. What is a simple credit?
4. Why can two learners describe the same picture with slightly different feelings?

## Summary
• Drawings, photographs, posters and video stills can all start a composition.
• Keep the story about 60 to 80 words and in logical order.
• Use the internet for pictures only with an adult, and say where the picture came from.

### Answers to practice
1. A textbook photograph, a poster, a newspaper picture, a comic, or a paused video. Any two are acceptable.
2. Ask a teacher or parent and use a site they have opened. Do not download from strangers or click prize links.
3. A short note such as 'Drawing by our group' or 'Photograph from our class textbook'.
4. A picture can suggest more than one careful reading. They should still stick to what the picture shows and listen to each other.

questions.question: Before writing a pictorial composition you should
options: hide the pictures
say what each picture shows and put them in order
click every link on the page
write the ending first and ignore the drawings
questions.explanation: Looking and ordering come before the sentences.

questions.question: In the email pictures, which order is logical?
options: Reply, send, compose, type
Compose, type, check and send, reply
Send, then compose, then delete the adult
Inbox first, with no message written
questions.explanation: A reply arrives only after a message has been composed and sent.

questions.question: Picture C, with a finger near Send, belongs
options: before anyone opens Compose
after typing and before the reply
after the story has ended
in a different subject
questions.explanation: Checking and sending sit between the typing and the reply.

questions.question: The story part of the composition should be about
options: 60 to 80 words
6 words
600 words
a password and a home address
questions.explanation: That is the length for this sub-strand. The title is extra.

questions.question: Which sentence best links two pictures?
options: First she clicked Compose. Then she typed the address.
Computer computer computer.
Password is 1234 and my home is here.
Suddenly the reply arrived before she wrote.
questions.explanation: First and Then keep the pictures in a possible order without sharing private information.

questions.question: If a draft is far too long, the writer should
options: add another unrelated story
cut repeated ideas and stay with the pictures
include a stranger's phone number
remove all the verbs
questions.explanation: The composition should stay near 60 to 80 words and follow the pictures.

questions.question: A video the class watches can help you write because
options: you can order moments you saw
you should copy any link in the corner
videos replace all sentences
you must download unknown files
questions.explanation: Paused moments work like pictures in a sequence.

questions.question: Looking online for pictures is safer when
options: you click every prize you see
a teacher or parent opens an approved site and stays with you
you send your address to get a download
you use a stranger's password
questions.explanation: Cyber safety means an adult chooses the site and you avoid unknown links.

questions.question: A credit in this lesson is
options: a loan of money
a short note saying where the picture came from
a password
the inbox
questions.explanation: Honesty about the source is enough at this level.

questions.question: Write one sentence that could match a picture of an adult and a child checking an email address.
questions.answer: Awuor and her aunt checked the address before she clicked Send.
questions.explanation: The sentence names the people and the safety check the picture shows.
